title: What's the deal with Voodoo?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore voodoo as a religion, starting with the 1791 Haitian slave uprising and the Bois Caiman-style voodoo ceremony that preceded it, and Pat Robertson's remarks after the Haiti earthquake. They cover the belief in a supreme god (Bondye) reached through loa (spirits, often ancestral), spirit possession (horse and rider), the African origins of voodoo in West Africa (word traced to the Fon language), the difference between voodoo and bo (black magic), the roles of the hungan and mambo, ceremonies with drumming, dance, and consecrated objects, Papa Legba as gatekeeper, syncretism with Catholicism under the French Code Noir, animal sacrifice practices, Western fear and misconceptions, public health concerns, the Marie Laveau legacy and the rise of hoodoo/Louisiana voodoo in New Orleans, and Hollywood portrayals such as White Zombie, Angel Heart, Serpent and the Rainbow, and Live and Let Die. The episode ends with listener mail about a former Guantanamo detainee and torture, and a request for practitioner feedback.

segments.title: Opening banter and the 1791 Haitian slave uprising
segments.summary: The hosts open with complaints, then go back in time to the August 1791 voodoo ceremony that preceded the Haitian slave uprising, and Pat Robertson's comments after the Haiti earthquake.

segments.title: What voodoo is: supreme god, loa and ancestors
segments.summary: Voodoo is described as a religion with no definitive holy text, a supreme god (Bondye in Haitian voodoo) reached through loa, spirits often based on ancestors. Comparisons to pagan religions are discussed.

segments.title: Voodoo priests, black magic (bo), and the good-community focus
segments.summary: Voodoo is described as mainly used for good. The dark side, bo, is distinguished from voodoo. Priests are called hungan (African) and mambo (Haitian), who are familiar with bo to oppose it.

segments.title: African origins and spirit possession
segments.summary: Voodoo's origins are traced to West Africa, with the word linked to the Fon language and the kingdoms of Fon and Congo. About thirty million people in Togo, Ghana and Benin practice it. Spirit possession, where a loa rides a 'horse', is a central tenet.

segments.title: Ceremonies, Papa Legba, and Catholic syncretism
segments.summary: Ceremonies feature percussion, song and dance, consecrated objects, and invoking Papa Legba, gatekeeper between worlds. Enslaved people in Haiti blended voodoo with Catholicism under the Code Noir, and loa are paired with saints such as St. Peter, St. James and St. Patrick.

segments.title: Animal sacrifice, possession dances and blood rituals
segments.summary: Animal sacrifice to appease spirits is described, including a test where a chicken or goat that eats the ritual dish is killed. Blood is mixed with rum, syrup and salt. The hooded dance of Gede-style possession and the immunity to pain during possession are described.

segments.title: Western fear, misconceptions, Marie Laveau and Hollywood
segments.summary: Western discomfort with blood, death and possession is discussed. Marie Laveau and her daughter in New Orleans, the split into factions, and the rise of hoodoo/who-do are covered. Hollywood films like White Zombie, Angel Heart, Serpent and the Rainbow and Live and Let Die are mentioned, along with the 1915-1935 Marine occupation of Haiti and public health concerns about bleeding and HIV.

segments.title: Listener mail: Guantanamo detainee and torture
segments.summary: A listener named Will writes about meeting an Australian former Guantanamo detainee who was subjected to extraordinary rendition and torture, and notes that Bagram has replaced Guantanamo as a secretive prison. The hosts ask practitioners to write in.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask voodoo practitioners to write in, mention social media and the website, and close the episode.
